introduction.title: Mathematics program review.
introduction.lead: A common assessment gives the department a shared view of mathematical readiness.
introduction.context: This report examines course, track, and class patterns, then turns question-level results into priorities for instruction and program review.

findings.title: Review the Geometry-to-Algebra II transition.
findings.evidence: Algebra II students answer 77% of Algebra questions correctly, compared with 46% of Geometry questions.
findings.implication: Check which geometric prerequisites need reinforcement, accounting for the demands of the individual tasks.

findings.title: Clarify what Honors placement should demonstrate.
findings.evidence: None of the four within-course track comparisons establishes a difference after adjustment for multiple comparisons.
findings.implication: That does not establish equivalence. Review common prerequisites and the additional depth expected in Honors.

findings.title: Investigate variation across Geometry classes.
findings.evidence: Regular Geometry class averages range from 52% to 67% on the same questions.
findings.implication: Compare incoming readiness, content exposure, and student work before deciding on support.

course-patterns.title: Readiness varies within every course.
course-patterns.lead: Average scores range from 48% in Algebra I to 82% in AP Calculus AB. Course membership alone does not describe an individual student’s readiness.
paragraphs: Start with the spread within each course. A group average can conceal students who need prerequisite support and students ready for greater challenge.

The main sequence tends toward higher scores in later courses, but these are different students assessed once. AP Statistics follows a separate pathway. Neither pattern measures growth or the effect of a course.
course-patterns.decision: Use short prerequisite checks to plan flexible support within each course. Do not assign students to tracks from this total score.

class-patterns.title: Begin the class review in Geometry.
class-patterns.lead: The three Regular Geometry classes average 52%, 52%, 67%. The 15.3-point spread warrants a closer look at what sits behind the totals.
paragraphs: Regular Geometry class R3 exceeds both R1 and R2 in the adjusted check across all 14 class comparisons. This reinforces the priority for review; it does not identify the cause of the difference.
Review the same question-level evidence with the Geometry team. Check whether classes had comparable opportunities to learn the assessed content and whether incoming readiness differed.
Collect recent student explanations and use a common scoring rubric. A recurring reasoning problem calls for a different response from unfamiliar content or an unusually difficult question.
Class and scheduled period are shown to help organize the review. These results do not isolate a teacher, timetable, or instructional effect.
class-patterns.decision: Agree on a common follow-up task and review student work together before changing grouping, pacing, or staffing.

comparisons.title: Track labels leave questions open.
comparisons.lead: Observed track gaps are uncertain. Treat the comparisons as prompts for program review, with confidence intervals alongside the estimates.
paragraphs: Within-course Honors-minus-Regular gaps range from -1.6 to +2.5 percentage points. All four are inconclusive after Holm adjustment; none meets the illustrative five-point equivalence criterion.

All four adjacent steps from Algebra I through AP Calculus show higher pooled averages under the student-level model. The first three intervals remain above zero in the section-cluster sensitivity check; AP Calculus has only one class, so its clustered comparison is not estimable. With few classes, these checks remain provisional.
Enrollment, prior readiness, and instructional exposure can explain part of a group difference. A common benchmark also samples only some of the depth a course may teach.
comparisons.decision: Define the common readiness evidence and extension work expected in each track. Review those expectations alongside classroom work.

content-areas.title: Look beneath the Algebra II total.
content-areas.lead: Algebra II averages 77% on Algebra questions and 46% on Geometry questions. That contrast directs attention to geometric readiness across the transition.
paragraphs: Algebra and Advanced Math each contain ten questions. Data Analysis and Geometry each contain five. Shorter domains are particularly sensitive to the choice of questions.
Compare groups on the same domain, then inspect its tasks. Differences between domains can reflect question difficulty and coverage; they are not differences on a common proficiency scale.
In Geometry, the assessment ranges from triangle angles to a circle with a constrained center. A single average cannot tell the department which of those demands is secure.
content-areas.decision: Select a small number of prerequisite skills for follow-up, using the question evidence and confirmed teaching sequence.

teaching-priorities.title: Check geometric readiness at the transition.
teaching-priorities.lead: The priority review pairs all five Geometry questions with two quadratic tasks. Darker cells mark lower accuracy and areas to examine first.
paragraphs: In Algebra II, 62% answer Q17 on triangle angles correctly; 26% answer Q26 on a constrained circle correctly. These questions make different demands. Use explanations to identify the barrier rather than treating the gap as lost learning.

Q4 asks students to identify a quadratic from a table (63% correct in Algebra II). Q10 asks which equivalent form reveals a minimum (51%). The contrast supports checking how students connect representations and structure.
The follow-up tasks below are proposed checks, not diagnoses inferred from a wrong answer. Confirm content exposure before deciding on reteaching.
teaching-priorities.decision: Agree on success criteria, teach to the observed need, and use fresh tasks to decide whether support should continue, change, or be reduced.

actions.title: Review the Geometry class spread.
actions.action: Compare incoming readiness, pacing, and opportunities to learn; then review a common task using the same rubric.
actions.evidence: Student explanations, taught-content records, and question-level results across the three Regular classes.
actions.review: At the next course-team review, identify which differences persist on common, recently taught content before changing provision.

actions.title: Test the reasoning behind priority tasks.
actions.action: Use short tasks on similarity, circle constraints, and equivalent quadratic forms; ask students to explain each representation.
actions.evidence: New task responses and worked explanations, scored against agreed criteria.
actions.review: At the end of the relevant teaching sequence, check transfer to a fresh context. Treat this as instructional follow-up, not an equated growth score.

actions.title: Make track expectations explicit.
actions.action: Define common prerequisites and Honors extension expectations; examine how current entry guidance reflects both.
actions.evidence: Shared essential tasks, extension work, teacher judgments, and the uncertainty in the benchmark comparisons.
actions.review: Before revising entry guidance, confirm that several sources of evidence support the proposed criteria. Do not use this benchmark as a placement cutoff.

teaching_checks: Distinguish a linear scale factor from an area factor.
Ask for a diagram and an explanation of why the factor is squared.
Q14, Q17 · Right triangles and angles
Check angle relationships and identification of the sides used in a sine ratio.
Use a rotated triangle and ask students to label the relevant sides before calculating.
Connect radius and center to the equation, then impose the extra constraint.
Ask students to explain each substitution before completing the calculation.
Connect a table and equivalent expressions to a function’s features.
Compare equivalent forms and ask which makes the minimum visible, and why.
